issue.issue_text: Whether the court is under an obligation to hear the accused on the question of sentence under section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: The case involved a comparison between Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), where the death penalty is an alternative to life imprisonment, and Section 303 IPC, which prescribed a mandatory death sentence for murder committed by a person already serving a life sentence.
law: Section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) grants the accused a right to be heard on the question of sentence after being convicted.
Section 354(3) of the CrPC requires the court to state special reasons for imposing a death sentence when it is an alternative to a lesser punishment.
application: The Court reasoned that the right to be heard on sentencing under Section 235(2) is a crucial safeguard, but its relevance is tied to the court having a choice or discretion in sentencing.

In cases under Section 302 IPC, where the court can choose between life imprisonment and death, the hearing is essential. It allows the accused to present mitigating circumstances to persuade the court to impose the lesser sentence.

Conversely, under Section 303 IPC, which mandated the death penalty, the court had no sentencing options. In such a scenario, the hearing under Section 235(2) becomes a "meaningless ritual" or an "idle formality" because the court is compelled by law to impose the death sentence regardless of what the accused says.
The Court held that the deprivation of this meaningful opportunity to be heard was a primary reason why Section 303 was harsh, arbitrary, and unjust.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the court is under an obligation to hear the accused on the question of sentence under Section 235(2) of the CrPC. This obligation is a fundamental right and a critical safeguard, particularly in cases where the court has the discretion to choose between different punishments, such as the death penalty and life imprisonment. The very fact that the denial of this right under the mandatory sentencing provision of Section 303 rendered that section unconstitutional underscores the importance and obligatory nature of the hearing.

law.fact_text: The death sentence is constitutionally valid if it is prescribed as an alternative penalty for an offense, not a mandatory one.

The Court's reasoning, referencing the Bachan Singh case, is that the constitutionality of the death penalty is preserved by the presence of judicial discretion, which allows a judge to consider the specific facts and circumstances of a case before imposing such an irrevocable punishment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court is under an obligation to hear the accused on the question of sentence under section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: The appellants/petitioners contended that section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code was applicable to the case and the Court was under an obligation to hear the accused on the question of sentence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the death sentence is constitutionally permissible.
appellant_arguments: The petitioners argued that the provision contained in section 303, which prescribes a mandatory death sentence, suffers from constitutional infirmities and is invalid.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that section 303 does not suffer from any constitutional infirmity, relying on the decision in Bachan Singh which upheld the validity of the death sentence. They contended that since section 303 does no more than prescribe the death sentence, it is constitutionally valid.

cases.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cases.principle: The word 'Law' in the expression 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 means the law must be right, just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive.
It upheld the constitutional validity of the death penalty and interpreted Article 21 in accordance with the interpretation from Maneka Gandhi.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 of the Constitution means the law must be right, just, and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive. If a procedure is arbitrary, it is no procedure at all and would be violative of Article 14.
obiter: The impossibility of laying down standards is at the very core of the criminal law as administered in India which invests the Judges with a very wide discretion in the matter of fixing the degree of punishment. The exercise of judicial discretion on well-recognised principles is, in the final analysis, the safest possible safeguard for the accused.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 303 of the Indian Penal Code is unconstitutional as it violates Article 21 of the Constitution. By mandating the death sentence for any person who commits murder while already under a sentence of life imprisonment, it prescribes a procedure for the deprivation of life that is unfair, unjust, and arbitrary. The provision is unconstitutional because it removes all judicial discretion, preventing the court from considering mitigating circumstances, and as a necessary consequence, it deprives the accused of the fundamental procedural safeguard under section 235(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code to be heard on the question of sentence.
legal_tests_applied: The procedure established by law for depriving a person of life or personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution must be fair, just, and reasonable.
A legal provision that makes a distinction in the matter of punishment between different classes of offenders must have a rational justification for that classification.
policy_considerations: A provision of law which deprives the court of the use of its wise and beneficent discretion in a matter of life and death, without regard to the circumstances in which the offence was committed, is harsh, unjust, and unfair.

The legislature cannot make relevant circumstances irrelevant, deprive the courts of their legitimate jurisdiction to exercise their discretion not to impose the death sentence in appropriate cases, and compel them to shut their eyes to mitigating circumstances.
So final, so irrevocable, and so irrestitutable is the sentence of death that no law which provides for it without the involvement of the judicial mind can be said to be fair, just, and reasonable.

There is no rational justification or social purpose for prescribing a mandatory sentence of death for a murder committed by a person under a sentence of life imprisonment for a prior, unrelated offence, such as forgery, as the motivation and nature of the two offences can be entirely different.

The classification between persons who commit murder while under a sentence of life imprisonment and those who are not is arbitrary and beyond the bounds of all reason for the purpose of making the death sentence mandatory for the former.
